scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that ethics matter for leadership, then argues 'highest' is too strict since skill matters too; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: We hope that the people who lead us are honest as well as capable.
Some people claim that to be an effective leader, a public official must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards.
I agree that good character matters greatly in a leader, but I believe the word highest sets too strict a test.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why ethics matter for leadership

sentences.text: First, strong moral standards genuinely help a leader to be effective.
Leaders whom people trust can unite them, win cooperation, and inspire honest effort.
For example, an official known for fairness and honesty is far more likely to be believed and followed.
This shows that good character builds the trust on which effective leadership depends.
A dishonest leader, by contrast, soon loses the loyalty and respect of the people.
Ethical conduct also sets an example that can raise the standards of a whole society.
To this extent, the claim rightly values morality in leadership.
Second, however, demanding the highest possible standards may be too strict to be useful.
Every human being has flaws, so a perfect leader has almost never existed.
Consider leaders with personal failings who still governed wisely and improved millions of lives.
Such cases show that effectiveness depends on skill and judgment as well as on character.
A leader of flawless morals but poor ability could still govern badly and fail the people.
Insisting on perfection might even rule out capable leaders for small, forgivable faults.
High standards, then, matter, but they are not the whole of effective leadership.
In conclusion, strong ethics are a vital part of being an effective leader.
But demanding the very highest standards ignores that skill and judgment matter too.
The best leaders combine sound character with the genuine ability to govern well.
